Module 04 · TypeScript for Frontend Engineers

Types That Make the
Wrong State Impossible

Four short lessons, all TypeScript — shapes, unions, types built from types, and the boundary where data comes in. Ending at the point where more types stop paying for themselves.
MODULE 04 · VIDEO 1
02 / 16
Lesson 1 · Structural typing

TypeScript does not care what you named it

Nominal (C++, Java, C#)

class Point { int x, y; };
class Vector { int x, y; };

Point p = Vector{1, 2};
// error: no viable conversion
// same shape, different name — rejected

Structural (TypeScript)

interface Point { x: number; y: number; }
interface Vector { x: number; y: number; }

const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 } as Vector;
const q: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 }; // fine, no cast
// same shape, any name (or no name) — assignable
A type is a shape, not a label. If a value has the right properties, it satisfies the type — whatever you called it, or didn't.

Lesson 1 · Types as sets

Every type is a set of valid values

A type isn't a container — it's a description of which values are legal. type Role = 'admin' | 'seeker' is a set with exactly two members. A union is the two sets combined; an object type is the set of every value shaped like it.

type Paths = '/admin/users' | '/admin/settings';
type Weird = false | 12 | 'hi'; // legal, if pointless
any sits outside this chart — it doesn't narrow anything, it turns the checker off. extends means "lower on this chart": array extends object, so an array is assignable wherever an object is expected.

Lesson 1 · unknown, any, never

Only one of these turns the checker off

TypeWhat you can do with itWhere it shows up
anyAnything, unchecked — a.b.c() compiles whether or not it exists.Giving up, or a boundary nobody typed yet.
unknownNothing, until you narrow it — every operation is rejected first.Data whose shape you genuinely don't know yet (a boundary you did think about).
neverNothing can be assigned to it, and it can't be reached.Exhaustiveness checks; the return type of a function whose only job is to throw.
fetch('/api/listings').then(r => r.json()) returns Promise<any> — the one place any sneaks back into a strict codebase uninvited.

Lesson 2 · Narrowing

The compiler re-checks every branch you write

typeof

if (typeof value === 'string') {
  value.trim(); // string here
}

in

if ('error' in state) {
  state.error; // has that field
}

a predicate

function isListing(x: unknown)
  : x is Listing {
  return typeof x === 'object'
    && x !== null
    && 'id' in x;
}
This isn't a runtime feature — it's TypeScript re-reading your if and shrinking the type for everything downstream of it. The check is exactly as good as the condition you wrote.

06 / 16
Lesson 2 · Discriminated unions

One tag, one exact shape per state

type ListingsRequest =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string }
  | { status: 'success'; data: Listing[] };

function describe(state: ListingsRequest) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'success': return state.data.length; // .data exists here, only here
    case 'error':   return state.error;
    default:         return null;
  }
}
Five booleans describe thirty-two states; this union describes exactly four. Narrow on status once and each branch gets only that state's fields — state.data is an error outside 'success'.

07 / 16
Lesson 2 · Exhaustiveness, for free

Add a state, the compiler finds every switch that forgot it

function assertNever(x: never): never {
  throw new Error('unhandled case');
}

function describe(state: ListingsRequest) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case 'success': return state.data.length;
    case 'error':   return state.error;
    case 'loading': return '…';
    case 'idle':    return null;
    default: return assertNever(state); // ❌ once a 5th status is added, this stops compiling
  }
}
Handle every case and what is left at default is never. Forget one later and the build fails at the exact switch that needs it.

Lesson 3 · Generics, plainly

A generic is a parameter — for a type

Same relationship as a function parameter: the caller doesn't know the value ahead of time, so the function doesn't either. A generic is the same deal for the type — the caller supplies it, usually by just calling the function normally.

function first<T>(list: T[]): T | undefined {
  return list[0];
}

function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(
  items: T[],
  keyFn: (item: T) => K
): Record<K, T[]> { /* … */ }

const byCompany = groupBy(listings, l => l.company); // T and K both inferred
You call groupBy(listings, …) like any function — TypeScript infers T and K from the arguments.

Lesson 3 · Constraining the parameter

keyof T only lets real keys in

function sortBy<T>(items: T[], key: keyof T): T[] {
  return [...items].sort((a, b) =>
    a[key] > b[key] ? 1 : -1);
}

sortBy(listings, 'postedAt');  // checked
sortBy(listings, 'salery');   // ❌ not a key of Listing
keyof T turns a type's own property names into a union — pass the wrong string and the compiler rejects it before the sort ever runs.

Lesson 3 · Utility types you'll actually reach for

Five that pay for themselves

UtilityRasmi example
Partial<T>type ListingDraft = Partial<Listing> — every field optional, mid-edit.
Required<T>type PublishedListing = Required<ListingDraft> — nothing left blank to go live.
Pick<T, K>type ListingCard = Pick<Listing, 'id' | 'title' | 'company'> — the feed only needs three fields.
Omit<T, K>type NewListing = Omit<Listing, 'id' | 'postedAt'> — the server assigns those two.
Record<K, T>type ByCompany = Record<string, Listing[]> — an index signature, typed on both sides.

Lesson 3 · Mapped types

[K in keyof T] is a for loop over a type

type FormErrors<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]?: string;
};

// FormErrors<Listing> walks every key of Listing
// and produces { title?: string; company?: string; … }
type Handlers<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `on${Capitalize<K & string>}Change`]:
    (value: T[K]) => void;
};
// { onTitleChange, onCompanyChange, … }
// keys renamed, not just mapped
The compiler runs this once, over the keys of a type, the way for...in runs once over the keys of an object — as lets you rename each key on the way through, not just keep it.

Lesson 4 · Typing async data

Promise<T> is where the lie gets a type

async function getListing(id: string): Promise<Listing> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/listings/${id}`);
  return res.json(); // Promise<any> — nothing checked this against Listing
}
The return type is a promise you made, not one the compiler verified. res.json() is typed any; TypeScript trusts your annotation and checks nothing underneath it. Same story for JSON.parse, localStorage and an untyped SDK — every boundary hands you any.

Lesson 4 · Schema validation at the boundary

Check it once, at the line where it enters

const ListingSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  title: z.string(),
  company: z.string(),
  remote: z.boolean(),
  salary: z.number().optional(),
});
MODULE 04 · VIDEO 4
14 / 16
Lesson 4 · Types on the inside

Infer the type from the schema — never write it twice

type Listing = z.infer<typeof ListingSchema>;

async function getListing(id: string): Promise<Listing> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/listings/${id}`);
  return ListingSchema.parse(await res.json()); // throws loudly if the shape is wrong
}
One definition does two jobs: a runtime check at the edge, a static type everywhere behind it. They can't drift out of sync — the type is derived from the schema, not written next to it by hand.

Lesson 4 · tsconfig, flag by flag

Strict mode is eight flags wearing one name

FlagWhat it catches
noImplicitAnyA parameter or variable that quietly became any because nothing typed it.
strictNullCheckslisting.company when listing could be undefined — the single biggest source of runtime crashes it removes.
strictFunctionTypesA callback parameter that's wider than the one it's replacing — unsound contravariance.
noUncheckedIndexedAccessbyCompany[name] typed as the value, not value | undefined — the lookup might fail and the type used to pretend otherwise.
exactOptionalPropertyTypesAssigning undefined to an optional field that was only ever supposed to be absent, not present-and-empty.
The baseline worth it: strict plus noUncheckedIndexedAccess. Past that, if a type is harder to read than the bug it would catch, write the simple version and stop.

  • Replace boolean soup with a discriminated unionexhaustiveness checking finds the state you forgot
